abstract: In addition to its canonical role as a selective barrier, the nuclear envelope is increasingly recognized as a dynamic structure, remodeled to integrate mechanical cues. Here, we discover that the bacterial pathogen Rickettsia parkeri deforms the nuclear envelope to an unprecedented degree to invade and exit human cell nuclei through large membrane protrusions. This extreme envelope remodeling is tolerated in part due to a bacterial protein that associates with the nuclear membrane and promotes nuclear infection, along with a mechanosensitive host enzyme that releases a signaling molecule from deformed nuclei. These findings establish a new mechanism of nucleocytoplasmic transport that redefines the size limits of nuclear envelope deformation cells can tolerate and resolves a long-standing question of how micron-scale cargo, such as bacteria, enter nuclei.
